# powerline-veg-risk

**Screening transmission corridors for vegetation risk from public
airborne LiDAR, in R.**

`vegrisk` is an R package plus two reproducible case studies. It takes
USGS 3DEP point clouds (LAS/LAZ) and OpenStreetMap power-line geometry
and produces a segment-by-segment screen for the two vegetation failure
modes utilities manage:

- **Grow-in:** canopy growing up into the clearance envelope beneath the
  conductors.
- **Fall-in:** “strike trees” beside the line that are tall enough to
  reach a conductor if they fall.

|  | Sunshine Canyon, CO | West Nashville, TN |
|----|----|----|
| Line | Sunshine–Boulder Hydro 115 kV, wood H-frames | TVA Maury–Davidson 500 kV, lattice towers, shared right-of-way |
| Setting | Wildland–urban interface (2010 Fourmile Canyon Fire burned ~2.5 km away) | Wooded hills, managed right-of-way |
| LiDAR | `CO_DRCOG_2020`, UTM metres, ~35 pts/m² | `TN_DavidsonCounty_D22`, Tennessee State Plane **US survey feet**, ~34 pts/m² |
| Delivered classes | ground / unclassified / noise only | \+ vegetation (3–5) and buildings (6) |
| Line length, above-ground points | 1.52 km, 2.26 M | 2.0 km, 1.05 M |
| Conductor returns found | 914 | 104,650 |
| Conductor elevation measured along | 2% of the line | **~100%** of the line |
| Result | Bounded: 3 robust grow-in candidates, 27 segments undecidable | Decisive: no grow-in, 24 strike trees in 7 segments, 32 clear |

## Headline findings

1.  **No public 3DEP project from 2019 on labels power lines.** I
    sampled the classification of all 641 USGS 3DEP projects from 2019
    onward in the public Entwine index. None uses the ASPRS wire
    classes; the few hits for codes 13/14 were topobathy datasets or
    state-specific reuse (NC Phase 4 uses 13 for roads). Conductor
    labels have to be derived.
2.  **Whether public LiDAR can decide grow-in depends on whether it
    sampled the conductors.** In Colorado it barely did, so the
    conductor is bounded within a band tens of metres tall and 27 of 30
    segments stay undecidable. In Nashville, the 500 kV bundles were
    sampled along almost the whole line, so the same pipeline gives a
    measured, decisive screen.
3.  **Vendor vegetation classes contain the conductors.** In Nashville,
    99.3% of conductor returns (103,918 points, 15–45 m up) are
    delivered as *high vegetation*. A canopy model built straight from
    the delivered classes flags **every one** of the 39 segments as
    grow-in; with conductor returns removed, none are.
4.  **Random cross-validation on point clouds misleads.** Random folds
    report a Colorado wire average precision of 0.22; 100 m spatial
    blocks report 0.004. A model trained in Colorado doesn’t transfer to
    Nashville (wire recall 0).

![Nashville risk map](reference/figures/nashville_risk_map.png)

Nashville risk map

## Pipeline

    3DEP tiles (TNM API) ─┐
                          ├─ clip to corridor ─ height-normalise (TIN on class 2)
    OSM lines (Overpass) ─┘                │
                                           ▼
              per-point features: multi-scale eigenvalue shape (k = 10, 30),
              echo structure, intensity percentile, height
                                           │
              weak labels from GIS + geometry (3DEP has no wire classes)
                                           │
              random forest (ranger), class-weighted, prior-corrected;
              spatially blocked CV vs random CV; feature ablation;
              vendor-class ground truth where it exists
                                           │
              conductor elevation: measured where seen, bounded elsewhere
                                           │
              canopy model from consensus vegetation, conductor returns removed
                                           │
              per 50 m segment: clearance encroachment + 3D strike trees
              under both conductor bounds, with a confidence label

| Step | Function | File |
|----|----|----|
| Find / download 3DEP tiles, fetch OSM layers | [`tnm_lidar_tiles()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/tnm_lidar_tiles.md), [`download_tiles()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/download_tiles.md), [`osm_power_lines()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_power_lines.md), [`osm_power_structures()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_power_structures.md), [`osm_buildings()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_buildings.md) | [R/fetch.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/fetch.R) |
| Corridor clip, noise removal, height normalisation, CRS-unit safety | [`read_corridor()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/read_corridor.md), [`line_corridor()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/line_corridor.md), [`las_m_per_unit()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/las_m_per_unit.md) | [R/preprocess.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/preprocess.R) |
| Point features | [`point_features()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/point_features.md) | [R/features.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/features.R) |
| Weak labels | [`weak_labels()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/weak_labels.md) | [R/labels.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/labels.R) |
| Classifier and validation | [`train_point_classifier()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/train_point_classifier.md), [`cv_point_classifier()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/cv_point_classifier.md), [`classify_probs()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/classify_probs.md), [`predict_points()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/predict_points.md), [`evaluate_vendor_classes()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/evaluate_vendor_classes.md) | [R/classify.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/classify.R) |
| Conductor model and risk | [`conductor_profile()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/conductor_profile.md), [`corridor_rasters()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/corridor_rasters.md), [`assess_risk()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/assess_risk.md) | [R/risk.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/risk.R) |
| Dry-season canopy greenness and moisture (optional) | [`landsat_scenes()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/landsat_scenes.md), [`landsat_composite()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/landsat_composite.md), [`canopy_dryness()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/canopy_dryness.md) | [R/landsat.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/landsat.R) |
| Fire-weather wind: windward strike trees, forecast watchlist (optional) | [`wind_history()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/wind_history.md), [`fire_wind_hours()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/fire_wind_hours.md), [`wind_fall_exposure()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/wind_fall_exposure.md), [`nws_forecast()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/nws_forecast.md), [`nws_alerts()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/nws_alerts.md), [`forecast_watchlist()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/forecast_watchlist.md) | [R/wind.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/wind.R) |
| Figures | [`plot_risk_map()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_risk_map.md), [`plot_profile()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_profile.md), [`plot_cross_section()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_cross_section.md), [`plot_cv()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_cv.md), [`plot_importance()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_importance.md), [`plot_canopy_dryness()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_canopy_dryness.md), [`plot_wind_exposure()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_wind_exposure.md) | [R/plot.R](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/R/plot.R) |
| Case studies | `run_case_study(cfg)` + one config script per site | [analysis/](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/analysis/) |

## Design decisions worth reading

**Distances are always metres.** Point clouds stay in their native CRS,
and every parameter is converted with
[`las_m_per_unit()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/las_m_per_unit.md).
The Nashville tiles are in US survey feet; without the conversion every
buffer would silently shrink 3.28×. Geographic CRSs are rejected.

**Labels are weak, and the code says so.** Training labels come from:

- **building:** OSM footprints, shrunk 1 m inward so crowns overhanging
  eaves don’t count as roof.
- **structure:** OSM pole and tower nodes.
- **wire:** an air-gap test (an elevated layer with empty space beneath
  it across a 3×3 m window) plus an **along-line run test** in
  chainage/offset coordinates: each conductor row must extend ≥ 12 m
  along *any* mapped line in the area, so second circuits on a shared
  right-of-way are labelled too. Crown tops are compact and fail.
- **vegetation:** everything else.

Elevated suspended candidates that fail the wire test, or that lie
beyond `wire_search_m` of any mapped line, **abstain** (NA) rather than
becoming “vegetation”, so missed and unmapped conductors aren’t taught
as trees. The mapped lines include OSM `power=minor_line` (distribution)
as well as `power=line`.

**Validation is spatial, and the gap is reported.** Folds are 100 m
spatial blocks; random folds are reported alongside. Precision is
measured at real class prevalence, and the headline metric is average
precision against its no-skill value. An ablation drops the features
that encode the labelling rule (height, echo structure).

**Class weighting is undone at prediction time.** The forest trains with
inverse-frequency case weights, i.e. under equal priors;
[`classify_probs()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/classify_probs.md)
multiplies by the true prevalence and renormalises. Without that, the
Colorado model called about 25,000 vegetation points “wire”.

**Conductor elevation is bounded, not guessed.**
[`conductor_profile()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/conductor_profile.md)
uses classified conductor returns where they pass sanity checks: more
than one mask radius from a structure (guy wires and crossarms are
linear too), a robust low quantile per 5 m bin, above the code minimum,
and at a plausible slope to neighbouring bins. Elsewhere it brackets the
conductor:

- **lower bound:** ground + NESC minimum clearance.
- **upper bound:** the chord between the supports either side, at
  ground + a maximum attachment height. A conductor sags below the chord
  between its attachments. Where the next support lies outside the data,
  the upper bound is reported as unknown.

Every risk metric is computed under both bounds, and each segment is
labelled `measured`, `robust` (same answer under both bounds) or
`bound-dependent`.

**Conductor returns are removed from the canopy model, but trees are
not.** Conductors that cross canopy aren’t “suspended”, so the rules
label them vegetation, and they would put “trees” at wire height under
the whole line.
[`corridor_rasters()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/corridor_rasters.md)
removes points inside the conductor envelope at or above the measured
conductor elevation only if they are wire-like:

- locally linear, or
- suspended: nothing in the 1.5 m layer just beneath the conductor band
  across a 3×3 m neighbourhood. Bundled 500 kV conductors form ribbons
  rather than lines, so this second test matters.

A crown that reaches wire height has foliage beneath it and stays, so it
is still flagged. The envelope comes from where conductor returns
actually are and is capped at the grow-in zone, so tall trees beside the
line keep their tops for the fall-in test. Cells emptied by the removal
are treated as unobserved, not bare ground.

**Unseen is not clear.** A cell with no canopy counts as bare ground
only if the LiDAR saw it. Two kinds of cell are unobserved instead:

- cells whose only above-ground returns were left out of the canopy
  model as uncertain: the unlabelled margins beside wires, structures
  and buildings, abstained near-line candidates, points the classifier
  and rules disagree on, and conductor-envelope removals;
- voids with no return of any class within 5 m, such as a missing tile,
  water or a dropout. The TIN terrain model bridges these, so without
  the check they would read as bare ground.

Each segment reports `frac_observed` (across the corridor) and
`frac_observed_under` (the grow-in zone). A segment that would be `none`
but has less than 75% of either observed is tiered `no data` (confidence
`low coverage` when that holds under both bounds), and the risk map
draws those grey and dotted. The pipeline also stops if a configured
tile is missing from The National Map.

**Fall-in uses 3D geometry and terrain.** A tree pivoting at its base
sweeps a sphere of radius *h*. It can strike if the 3D distance from its
base to the nearest conductor point (DTM at the tree, modelled conductor
elevation, measured outer-phase offset) is ≤ *h*. Trees inside the
grow-in zone count as grow-in, not strike.

**Structures are masked.** Towers, H-frames and crossarms otherwise look
like tall trees under the conductors. Cells within a structure-sized
radius of OSM structure nodes and line vertices (for every circuit in
the corridor) are masked (known structures: not scored, but not counted
as data gaps), and features one or two cells wide are removed with a 3×3
crown-support filter.

**LiDAR says where canopy has grown in; Landsat says how green and wet
it is.** The grow-in screen ranks canopy by its distance to the
conductor, not by how readily it would carry fire to the line. An
optional Landsat step adds that:

- **Data:** Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2 surface reflectance, from
  the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API (no key needed). Only the
  corridor window of each cloud-optimised GeoTIFF is read.
- **Composite:** a per-pixel median over every clear dry-season
  observation in the chosen years. `QA_PIXEL` masks fill, cloud, dilated
  cloud, cirrus, shadow, snow and water. Water is masked because its
  negative NDVI would read as very dry canopy. Two indices come out:
  **NDVI** (greenness) and **NDMI** (NIR against SWIR1: canopy water
  content, the closer of the two to fuel moisture).
- **LiDAR picks the pixels.** A 30 m pixel is wider than many
  rights-of-way, so most pixels mix trees with cleared ground. Each
  pixel gets a canopy fraction from the 1 m CHM, and pixels under 50%
  canopy are not scored. A segment’s value is the mean of its pixels,
  weighted by how many of the segment’s canopy cells *inside the grow-in
  zone* fall in each one. It describes the trees under the wires, not
  the forest beside them.
- **Relative, not absolute.** Neither index has a fire-danger threshold.
  Each segment is ranked against every canopy pixel in the corridor, and
  `dry_canopy` marks the lowest quarter. `dry_grow_in` is dry *and*
  grown in under the optimistic conductor bound; `dry_grow_in_lo` uses
  the pessimistic tier.

**Weather can’t tell segments apart, but wind direction can.**
Fire-weather grids are 2.5–25 km wide, so every segment of a short line
gets the same wind. The spatial signal comes from combining wind
*direction* with where each strike tree stands. Windthrown trees fall
roughly downwind, so a tree on the upwind side of the line in dry,
high-wind hours matters more than the same tree on the downwind side.

- **Fire-weather hours:** ten years of hourly ERA5 reanalysis
  (Open-Meteo, no key). Hours count as fire weather when gusts are in
  the record’s top 5% and relative humidity is ≤ 30%.
- **Hitting arc, from the existing reach test.** A tree of height *h*,
  with its base a horizontal distance *d* from the outer phase and the
  conductor *dz* above its base, reaches horizontally *R* = √(*h*² −
  *dz*²) at conductor height. It hits if it falls within acos(*d*/*R*)
  of straight at the line. There is no arbitrary angle cutoff, apart
  from a ±15° allowance for the scatter of real fall directions.
- **Per tree:** the share of fire-weather hours whose wind would throw
  it into that arc (`wind_hit_lo` / `wind_hit_hi`). **Per segment:** the
  windward strike-tree count, and the expected number thrown towards the
  line in a fire-weather hour. Wind directions are rotated from true to
  grid north first.
- **Forecast watchlist:** `analysis/watchlist.R` applies the same
  thresholds and geometry to the live NWS 7-day hourly forecast and
  active Red Flag Warnings. It lists the segments whose strike trees the
  coming winds would throw, plus dry grown-in segments, and when.

## Case study 1: Sunshine Canyon, Colorado

![Sunshine conductor
profile](reference/figures/sunshine_conductor_profile.png)

Sunshine conductor profile

**The conductor is barely sampled.** After the sanity checks, conductor
returns survive along 2% of the line, and spans run 257–468 m between
H-frames across a 250 m descent into the canyon. Along 22% of the line
the next support is outside the data, so there is no upper bound at all.

|  | optimistic conductor (upper bound) | pessimistic conductor (code minimum) |
|----|----|----|
| segments with ≥ 5 m² of canopy in the clearance envelope | **3 of 30** | 28 of 30 |
| potential strike trees | 19 | 307 |

- **3 robust grow-in candidates.** The top one (about 1.01–1.06 km along
  the line, conductor measured along 41% of it) has a conductor about 15
  m up, leaving a low H-frame on the canyon floor, beside riparian
  cottonwoods up to 27 m tall. The other two have trees of 20–29 m that
  exceed even the highest plausible conductor. They are the places to
  verify with imagery or a field visit first.
- **27 segments are bound-dependent.** Whether they need work depends on
  where the conductor actually is, which this acquisition doesn’t show.
- **The LiDAR saw the corridor.** Every segment has at least 94% of its
  corridor and 85% of its grow-in zone observed (median 100%), so none
  is tiered `no data`.

| class | n | prevalence | avg. precision, spatial blocks | random folds | spatial, no height/echo |
|----|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| building | 3,608 | 0.0016 | 0.36 | 0.85 | 0.51 |
| structure | 1,602 | 0.0007 | 0.012 | 0.41 | 0.011 |
| wire | 914 | 0.0004 | 0.004 | 0.22 | 0.005 |

With only a few hundred metres of labelled conductor and five
structures, wires and structures don’t generalise across space here.
Random folds would have hidden that.

![Sunshine cross-section](reference/figures/sunshine_cross_section.png)

Sunshine cross-section

**The grown-in canopy is not the dry canopy.** A dry-season
(July–September) median of 25 Landsat 8 scenes from 2019–2021,
bracketing the 2020 flight, gives 142 canopy-dominated 30 m pixels in
the corridor. 23 of the 30 segments have enough grown-in canopy to rank;
NDVI and NDMI agree closely across them (r = 0.89).

| robust grow-in candidate | NDVI percentile | NDMI percentile |
|----|---:|---:|
| 0.10–0.15 km, trees to 20 m | 0.37 | 0.49 |
| 1.01–1.06 km, riparian cottonwoods on the canyon floor (top candidate) | 0.50 | 0.80 |
| 1.06–1.11 km, canyon floor, trees to 29 m | 0.89 | 0.96 |

- **None of the 3 robust grow-in candidates is dry.** The two worst
  encroachments are among the wettest canopy on the line: riparian trees
  on the canyon floor.
- **The 5 driest segments** (lowest NDVI quarter; 0.05–0.10, 0.46–0.51,
  0.81–0.86 and 1.32–1.42 km) are all bound-dependent: grow-in only if
  the conductor is at the code minimum. If the conductor turns out to be
  low there, encroachment and dry fuel coincide, so these come first
  among the 27 undecidable segments.

![Sunshine canopy
dryness](reference/figures/sunshine_canopy_dryness.png)

Sunshine canopy dryness

**Fire-weather winds come from one direction, and that splits the strike
trees in two.** Over 2015–2024 there were 609 fire-weather hours (gusts
≥ 15.2 m/s, RH ≤ 30%), two-thirds of them in October–December. 94% came
from the west: the Front Range downslope winds behind the 2021 Marshall
Fire. The line runs south-west to north-east, so those winds blow trees
west of it towards the conductors and trees east of it away.

|  | potential strike trees | windward (≥ 50% of fire-weather hours) | expected thrown towards the line per fire-weather hour |
|----|---:|---:|---:|
| pessimistic conductor (code minimum) | 307 | 126 | 127 |
| optimistic conductor (upper bound) | 19 | 10 | 10 |

- **The split is close to all-or-nothing.** Windward trees are hit in
  95% of fire-weather hours on average; the median leeward tree is hit
  in 1%.
- **Under the optimistic bound, the top grow-in candidate also has the
  most windward strike trees:** 7 of its 13, at 1.01–1.06 km. It is the
  segment to verify first on both counts.
- **The dry segment at 1.32–1.37 km** (lowest NDVI on the line) has 9
  strike trees under the pessimistic bound, all windward.

![Sunshine wind exposure](reference/figures/sunshine_wind_exposure.png)

Sunshine wind exposure

## Case study 2: West Nashville, Tennessee

![Nashville conductor
profile](reference/figures/nashville_conductor_profile.png)

Nashville conductor profile

**The conductor is measured along the whole line.** The 500 kV bundles
were well sampled: 104,650 conductor returns, three phases at about −12,
0 and +12 m, and a second circuit sharing the right-of-way at +30–45 m.
The profile shows clean catenaries between towers, about 15–45 m above
the ground (median 24 m).

**Classifier against weak labels (spatial blocks):**

| class | n | prevalence | avg. precision, spatial blocks | random folds | spatial, no height/echo |
|----|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| wire | 104,650 | 0.10 | **0.88** | 0.94 | 0.83 |
| structure | 4,262 | 0.004 | 0.03 | 0.26 | 0.02 |

![Nashville
cross-validation](reference/figures/nashville_cv_metrics.png)

Nashville cross-validation

Wires transfer across space here: average precision 0.88 against a
no-skill 0.10, and 0.83 even without the height and echo features that
encode the labelling rule. Structures (31 lattice towers) still don’t.

**Against the vendor’s classes.** These are independent of the weak
labels. A geometric conductor zone (inside the measured conductor
envelope, within 3 m of the conductor or above) is excluded from scoring
for every method alike, because the vendor put conductors in vegetation.
Vegetation is 98.5% of the scored points, so its F1 can’t show skill:
predicting “vegetation” everywhere scores 0.992.

|  | vegetation F1 | building F1 | balanced accuracy | Cohen’s κ |
|----|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| always “vegetation” (baseline) | 0.992 | 0 | 0.50 | 0 |
| weak labels | 0.950 | 0 | 0.46 | −0.01 |
| model trained on weak labels | 0.957 | 0 | 0.47 | −0.01 |
| Colorado model, transferred | 0.992 | 0 | 0.50 | 0.00 |
| **trained on vendor labels (spatial CV)** | 0.998 | **0.88** (AP 0.95) | 0.89 | — |

- **On vegetation vs building, the weak-label pipeline has no skill at
  this site.** OSM maps one building in the corridor, so there are no
  building labels to learn from. The vendor’s labels would buy a
  building F1 of 0.88. The weak models’ lower vegetation recall is
  mostly second-circuit conductors and abstentions, which the vendor
  also calls vegetation.
- **The Colorado model doesn’t transfer.** With its own class prior it
  recalls 0% of Nashville’s conductor returns. Threshold-free, its wire
  average precision is 0.22 against a 0.10 baseline (the Nashville
  model: 0.87). Its 0.992 vegetation F1 is exactly the baseline.

**Risk screen.** The same segments, with three different canopy models:

| canopy model | grow-in | fall-in | clear |
|----|---:|---:|---:|
| vendor vegetation classes, as delivered | 39 | 0 | 0 |
| vendor vegetation + this package’s conductor removal | 0 | 10 | 29 |
| **this package** (consensus vegetation + conductor removal) | **0** | **7** | **32** |

- **The delivered classes would send crews to every span.** Removing
  conductor returns is the whole grow-in correction (39 → 0). Consensus
  labelling (model and weak rules agreeing on vegetation, vendor
  buildings removed) then trims fall-in from 10 segments to 7.
- **No grow-in.** The managed right-of-way is clear under the
  conductors.
- **The 32 clear segments were seen, not assumed.** Every segment has at
  least 91% of its corridor and of its grow-in zone observed (median
  99%), so none is tiered `no data`. The lowest segment (0.36–0.41 km,
  91% under the line) is still 16 points above the 75% threshold.
- **24 strike trees across 7 segments,** 28–39 m from the centreline,
  the same under both bounds because the conductor is measured. They are
  the list to verify.
- **The conductor envelope has to cover every phase.** An earlier run
  capped it at 15 m while one outer phase sits up to ~19 m from the OSM
  centreline. That left outer-phase returns in the canopy model, which
  showed up as 2 grow-in segments and 4 extra strike trees at the
  envelope edge. Widening the grow-in zone to 21 m removed all of them.

![Nashville
cross-section](reference/figures/nashville_cross_section.png)

Nashville cross-section

## Limitations

- **Weak labels.** Wire and structure accuracy is agreement with the
  labelling rules. Nashville’s vendor classes give real ground truth for
  vegetation and buildings only, and they themselves misclassify
  conductors. A hand-labelled test set (e.g. in CloudCompare) is the
  next step.
- **Bounds rest on assumptions.** Attachment heights are capped (20 m
  for the H-frames, 45 m for the lattice towers), and every support is
  assumed to be an OSM vertex or tagged node. A taller or unmapped
  structure would invalidate the upper bound locally.
- **Wire labels are trusted.** A wire label requires an observed air gap
  beneath it, so cells holding only wire-labelled returns count as
  observed bare ground. A thin branch layer within the label’s 4 m layer
  under a conductor can join the wire label and drop out of the canopy
  model.
- **Conductor removal is a judgement.** Canopy within ~1.5 m beneath a
  conductor can’t be told apart from a conductor over dense canopy; both
  are kept as canopy and flagged as grow-in, which is the conservative
  choice.
- **Second circuits** are labelled and their towers masked, but only the
  study line gets a conductor profile; second-circuit returns over
  canopy can remain in the canopy model beyond the study line’s
  envelope.
- **Conductors OSM doesn’t map** (telecom and communication lines,
  unmapped circuits) are not labelled wire. Where they hang free they
  abstain and stay out of the canopy model; where they cross canopy they
  look like foliage and are kept as canopy, like any conductor over a
  crown.
- **OSM geometry** is volunteer-digitised. Conductor envelopes are sized
  from where returns actually are, not from the centreline alone.
- **The structure mask** hides canopy close to each support, so strike
  trees right beside structures are not scored.
- **Treetops from a CHM** (local maxima, 5 m window) merge or split
  crowns in dense stands.
- **Vertical units** are assumed to match horizontal units (true for
  both deliveries: metres/metres and US survey feet/US survey feet).
- **Landsat greenness is not fuel moisture.** Low NDVI over canopy can
  also mean thin, trimmed or leaf-off crowns, and a 30 m pixel always
  mixes the right-of-way with its edges. `dry_canopy` ranks segments
  within one corridor and one composite. It can’t be compared across
  sites or seasons, and it is not a fire-danger rating.
- **Reanalysis wind is regional.** ERA5 resolves the synoptic flow at
  10–25 km, not channelling along a canyon or speed-up over a ridge, and
  its gusts are a model diagnostic. The watchlist applies thresholds
  from that record to NWS forecast gusts, which are a different product,
  so treat the gust threshold as a starting point to tune per site.
  Trees are assumed to fall downwind, within ±15°; trees that break or
  lean, or limbs, can do otherwise.

## Reproduce

``` r

# R >= 4.3
install.packages(c("lidR", "sf", "terra", "lwgeom", "ranger", "FNN", "data.table",
                   "httr2", "units", "withr", "ggplot2", "scales", "devtools"))
```

``` bash
Rscript analysis/run_sunshine_canyon.R   # ~0.6 GB of 3DEP LiDAR on first run
Rscript analysis/run_nashville.R         # ~0.3 GB; uses the Colorado model for the transfer test
Rscript analysis/watchlist.R sunshine    # live NWS forecast against a finished run (needs `wind` in the config)
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'           # unit tests: synthetic geometry + lidR example data, no network
```

Cross-validation is the slow part (minutes on mains power, much longer
on battery). Set `VEGRISK_REUSE=1` to reuse a site’s saved model and
validation results and recompute only labels and risk. The OSM layers
used are cached in `data-raw/<site>/*.geojson`, so reruns are
reproducible even if OSM changes. Outputs go to `output/<site>/`:
`segments.gpkg`, `trees.gpkg`, `segments.csv`, `conductor_profile.csv`,
`cv_metrics.csv`, `summary.rds`. A site config with
`landsat = list(years, months)` also writes `landsat_composite.tif` and
`landsat_scenes.csv`; the composite is cached and reused on reruns.
`wind = list(start, end)` writes and reuses `wind_hourly.csv`; the
watchlist writes `watchlist.csv`.

## Data

- **LiDAR:** U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program, public domain:
  `CO_DRCOG_2020_B20` tiles `w0472n4429`, `w0472n4430`;
  `TN_DavidsonCounty_D22` tiles `155020`, `155060`, `155100`, `155140`,
  `169020`.
- **Power lines, structures, buildings:** © OpenStreetMap contributors,
  ODbL.
- **Landsat:** U.S. Geological Survey Landsat 8–9 Collection 2 Level-2
  surface reflectance, public domain, accessed through the Microsoft
  Planetary Computer.
- **Historical wind:** Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis via the
  [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/) historical weather API, CC BY
  4.0.
- **Forecasts and alerts:** U.S. National Weather Service API
  (api.weather.gov), public domain.

# Package index

## Data acquisition

- [`tnm_lidar_tiles()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/tnm_lidar_tiles.md)
  : Find USGS 3DEP LiDAR point-cloud tiles intersecting an area of
  interest
- [`download_tiles()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/download_tiles.md)
  : Download LiDAR tiles, skipping files already present
- [`osm_power_lines()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_power_lines.md)
  : Fetch overhead power lines from OpenStreetMap
- [`osm_power_structures()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_power_structures.md)
  : Fetch power-line support structures (poles, towers) from
  OpenStreetMap
- [`osm_buildings()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/osm_buildings.md)
  : Fetch building footprints from OpenStreetMap

## Corridor point cloud

- [`read_corridor()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/read_corridor.md)
  : Read the corridor point cloud and normalise heights
- [`line_corridor()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/line_corridor.md)
  : Build a corridor polygon around power lines
- [`las_m_per_unit()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/las_m_per_unit.md)
  : Metres per horizontal CRS unit of a LAS object or file header

## Classification

- [`point_features()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/point_features.md)
  : Compute per-point classification features
- [`rule_proxy_features`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/rule_proxy_features.md)
  : Features that directly encode the wire-labelling rule
- [`weak_labels()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/weak_labels.md)
  : Assign weak labels to featurised points
- [`assign_blocks()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/assign_blocks.md)
  : Assign points to spatial blocks and CV folds
- [`train_point_classifier()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/train_point_classifier.md)
  : Train a random-forest point classifier
- [`cv_point_classifier()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/cv_point_classifier.md)
  : Cross-validate the point classifier: spatial blocks vs random folds
- [`classify_probs()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/classify_probs.md)
  : Prior-corrected class probabilities
- [`evaluate_vendor_classes()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/evaluate_vendor_classes.md)
  : Score labels against vendor-delivered ASPRS classes
- [`predict_points()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/predict_points.md)
  : Classify all featurised points

## Conductor model and risk

- [`segment_lines()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/segment_lines.md)
  : Split power lines into equal-length segments
- [`line_vertex_points()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/line_vertex_points.md)
  : Line vertices as candidate structure locations
- [`corridor_rasters()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/corridor_rasters.md)
  : Build terrain and vegetation-only canopy height rasters
- [`conductor_profile()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/conductor_profile.md)
  : Model conductor elevation along the line
- [`assess_risk()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/assess_risk.md)
  : Locate trees and score grow-in / fall-in risk per segment

## Canopy greenness and moisture (Landsat)

- [`landsat_scenes()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/landsat_scenes.md)
  : Find Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 scenes over an area of interest
- [`landsat_composite()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/landsat_composite.md)
  : Median dry-season NDVI and NDMI composite from Landsat scenes
- [`canopy_dryness()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/canopy_dryness.md)
  : Dry-season greenness and moisture of grown-in canopy, per segment

## Fire-weather wind

- [`wind_history()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/wind_history.md)
  : Hourly historical wind and humidity for a corridor
- [`fire_wind_hours()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/fire_wind_hours.md)
  : Select dry, high-wind ("fire-weather") hours
- [`wind_fall_exposure()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/wind_fall_exposure.md)
  : Which strike trees the fire-weather winds would throw into the line
- [`nws_forecast()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/nws_forecast.md)
  : Hourly National Weather Service forecast for a corridor
- [`nws_alerts()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/nws_alerts.md)
  : Active NWS watches, warnings and advisories at a corridor
- [`forecast_watchlist()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/forecast_watchlist.md)
  : Segments to watch under the coming fire weather

## Figures

- [`plot_canopy_dryness()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_canopy_dryness.md)
  : Map of dry-season canopy greenness and dry grown-in segments
- [`plot_cross_section()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_cross_section.md)
  : Cross-section of classified points perpendicular to the line
- [`plot_cv()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_cv.md)
  : Cross-validation metrics: spatial-block vs random folds
- [`plot_importance()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_importance.md)
  : Permutation importance of the top features
- [`plot_profile()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_profile.md)
  : Ground and conductor profile along the line
- [`plot_risk_map()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_risk_map.md)
  : Map of canopy height, segment priority, and strike trees
- [`plot_wind_exposure()`](https://mjorden.github.io/powerline-veg-risk/reference/plot_wind_exposure.md)
  : Strike trees the fire-weather winds would throw into the line
